name: Khmer Empire
capital: Yasodharapura (Angkor); earlier Hariharalaya and Koh Ker
summary: A powerful Hindu-Buddhist empire of mainland Southeast Asia, builder of Angkor Wat, supported by huge water-management systems.

location.value: Centred on the “hydraulic cities” around Angkor in northern Cambodia. At its height it ruled or held as vassals most of mainland Southeast Asia, reaching north towards southern China.

terrain.value: The Tonlé Sap lake and Mekong floodplain, with the Kulen hills as a water source.

climate.value: Monsoonal. Strong monsoon rains followed by severe droughts in the 14th–15th centuries damaged the hydraulic system and may have pushed people south.

resources.value: Rice (up to three harvests a year with irrigation), fish from the Tonlé Sap (prahok), and forest products.

disasters.value: Alternating droughts and floods. Deforestation of the Kulen hills added to the strain on the water system.

population.value: Not stated in the infobox. Angkor is often estimated to have had several hundred thousand people. Estimates vary widely.

urbanisation.value: Angkor’s water network (peak 11th–13th centuries) was “the most extensive pre-industrial urban complex in the world”. The East Baray reservoir measured 7.1 × 1.7 km.

disease.value: Plague has been suggested as a factor in Angkor’s decline, but this theory has been reconsidered.

migration.value: After 1431 the court and population moved south towards the Phnom Penh area. The abandonment of Angkor may have been only partial.

economicBase.value: Irrigated rice farming organised around temples, plus fishing and market trade, which women largely ran (according to Zhou Daguan).

tradeRoutes.value: Overland and river trade in mainland Southeast Asia, and sea trade with China, Java, Srivijaya and South India.

wealth.value: No GDP estimate exists. Its wealth is visible in temple building.

moneyAndTax.value: No money at first: barter was the main exchange from the 9th to 12th centuries. By the 13th century Chinese cash coins, cloth, gold and silver were in use. Officials taxed each market stall.

inequality.value: A Hindu-influenced hierarchy, with the god-king and Brahmin priests at the top and slaves at the bottom. Commoners were the majority.

governmentType.value: A monarchy with a devaraja (god-king) cult. Kings were seen as divine and responsible for the irrigation system.

keyRulers.value: Jayavarman II (founder, consecrated 802). Yasovarman I (founded Yasodharapura). Suryavarman II (1113–1150, built Angkor Wat). Jayavarman VII (1181–1218, built Angkor Thom and the Bayon). Ponhea Yat (last at Angkor, 1394–1431).

succession.value: Often contested: several kings took the throne by force. The capital moved several times (Hariharalaya, Yasodharapura, Koh Ker, back to Yasodharapura).

institutions.value: Temple foundations managed land, labour and rice. A hierarchy of officials and priests. Stone inscriptions recorded grants and laws.

stability.value: Periods of civil war, such as the decade of three rival kings before Suryavarman I (early 11th century). The Cham sack of Angkor in 1177.

eliteConflict.value: Usurpations and rival claimants were common. Religious shifts (Hindu versus Buddhist kings) also caused conflict, e.g. Jayavarman VIII opposing Buddhism.

armyAndTech.value: Infantry, war elephants and river fleets, depicted on temple reliefs. Army sizes are unknown; oral claims of millions are not credible.

majorWars.value: Repeated wars with Champa (the Cham captured Angkor in 1177; Jayavarman VII won in 1203), with Đại Việt, and later with Sukhothai and Ayutthaya, which besieged Angkor in 1352 and 1393–94 and took it in 1431.

territoryChange.value: About 1,000,000 km² around 1290 (Wikipedia infobox). Lost eastern territories after 1220 and western lands to the Thai kingdoms.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals were Champa, Đại Việt, Sukhothai and Ayutthaya. Diplomatic and trade ties with China and South India.

inventions.value: Large-scale hydraulic engineering (barays, canals), sandstone temple-mountain architecture, and bronze casting.

scienceEducation.value: Sanskrit learning among priests and temple schools. Astronomy was used in temple alignment. General literacy is unknown.

openness.value: Adopted Indian religions, scripts and political ideas, and later Theravada Buddhism from Sri Lanka.

religion.value: Hinduism (Shiva and Vishnu) as the main state religion. Mahayana Buddhism under Jayavarman VII. Theravada Buddhism dominant by the 13th–14th centuries.

languageWriting.value: Old Khmer (everyday and administrative) and Sanskrit (religious), written in Khmer script. The last dated Sanskrit inscription is from 1327.

artsArchitecture.value: Angkor Wat (built 1113–1150), the Bayon, Banteay Srei, and vast bas-reliefs. Angkor Wat is the world’s largest religious monument.

socialStructure.value: King, Brahmin priests, nobility and officials, commoners (the majority), and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: The god-king cult and temple religion. Angkor Wat is today the symbol of Cambodia and appears on its flag.

neighbours.value: Champa, Đại Việt, Sukhothai, Ayutthaya, Lan Xang, the Mon kingdoms and Srivijaya.

ideasReligions.value: Received Hinduism and Buddhism from India and Sri Lanka. The Chinese envoy Zhou Daguan (1296–97) wrote The Customs of Cambodia, a key source.

colonisation.value: As an empire it held vassal states across mainland Southeast Asia. It was never colonised. Its successor, Cambodia, became a French protectorate in 1863.

riseSignals.value: Jayavarman II unified Khmer principalities and declared independence in 802. Irrigation-based rice surpluses supported large populations and temple-building.

peakPeriod.value: 12th–13th centuries, under Suryavarman II (Angkor Wat) and Jayavarman VII (Angkor Thom).

declineSignals.value: Climate swings that wrecked the water system, a shift to Theravada Buddhism away from the god-king cult, power struggles, and attacks from Ayutthaya.

outcome.value: Transformation. After Ayutthaya captured Angkor in 1431, Ponhea Yat moved the court south towards Phnom Penh. Post-Angkor Cambodia continued as a smaller kingdom.

sources.value: Stone inscriptions, temple reliefs, archaeology (including LiDAR surveys), and Chinese accounts. No other written records survive. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026 (the article carries a citation-needed warning). See also Chandler (2008).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. Rulers and temples are well dated. Population, the reasons for the decline, and the meaning of “Java” in the founding inscription are debated. Reign dates differ slightly between sources.
